title.full: ASEAN Green Future Project Phase 2.2 Report, Analysis and Modelling of Power Sector in Thailand

publisher.full: Sustainable Development Solutions Network and ClimateWorks Centre

description: Thailand-specific pathway with a least-cost approach to minimizing power sector emissions by 2060.
pathwayDescription:
The Near Zero Emission (NZE) scenario from the ASEAN Green Future project is a normative pathway that reduces Thailand’s GHG emissions from the power sector as much as possible by 2060, based on a least-cost optimization using the LEAP-NEMO modeling framework. Some restrictions are implemented, including limits on renewable energy installed capacity by different energy sources. This constrains renewable energy sources to 70% of total electricity generation in 2050.

The NZE scenario is an optimistic outlook that models a faster ramp-up of renewable energy than is currently targeted in Thailand’s power and energy plans. It assumes some new technologies can be scaled to reduce power sector emissions starting in the 2030s, namely clean hydrogen and carbon capture and storage (CCS). By 2037, natural gas (including CCS) contributes only 30% of installed power capacity in the NZE scenario, whereas gas-fired power capacity still accounts for 39% and 42% of total capacity in the accompanying MAP and EXT scenarios, respectively. By 2050, natural gas contributes 18% of total capacity in the NZE scenario, and coal capacity is completely phased out.

The ASEAN Green Future regional research project is run by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network, Climateworks Centre, and local researchers from leading universities. The project develops national policy analysis and near-zero pathways that are meant to provide policy recommendations and support policymakers.

coreDrivers.policies: Near-zero policy and constraint assumptions drive NZE: fossil power phaseouts, 70% renewable electricity by 2050, CCUS and hydrogen from 2030, and strong transport/end-use electrification.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: The pathway targets the lowest feasible GHG emissions in the power sector by 2060; it is near-zero but not net zero.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Technology unit costs are a core driver because LEAP-NEMO selects least-cost capacity expansion and dispatch under given technology constraints. This means that declining costs for solar, wind, gas with CCS, and hydrogen power capacity affects deployment rates.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: The pathway follows projections based on the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 2, with GDP growing 3% p.a., with population, household, and urbanization numbers based on UN projections and official Thai statistics. Sectoral value-added projections are based on World Bank indicators, assuming they remain stable. All these indicators are common demand drivers rather than pathway-specific differentiators.

dependencies.dependency_description: NZE is not feasible without strong policy design, including coal power phaseout by 2050 and oil/diesel power phaseout by 2030. This helps reach the 70% renewable electricity by 2050 target.
NZE requires stronger regulatory intervention than the EXT and MAP pathways to enforce fossil fuel based power phaseouts and advanced-technology market entry.
NZE depends on large end-use uptake assumptions that reshape power demand, especially EVs, hydrogen vehicles, electric rail, efficient appliances, and electric cooking.

NZE requires very large system buildout and integration—about 186.87 GW of capacity by 2060, including 65 GW solar, 45 GW wind, 15 GW gas-CCS, hydrogen power, imports, and grid modernization—making infrastructure more binding than in the EXT and MAP pathways.

NZE relies on technologies not used in EXT/MAP, especially natural gas with CCS and clean hydrogen power starting in 2030, alongside steep renewable deployment and fuel-economy/efficiency improvements.

NZE explicitly uses maximum-capacity constraints and reaches a plateau because of renewable potential and fossil-fuel limits. Solar, wind, biomass, and hydro potential as well as electricity imports become material system constraints.
